topic.label: EEG & Signal Methods
topic.description: EEG signal processing, sleep staging, neural time series, modeling, and practical analysis methods.

papers.title: The Wild West of Nomenclature, Definitions, and Methodologies in Rodent Sleep Scoring.
papers.abstract: Rodent models are essential for investigating the mechanisms and regulation of sleep, yet the field lacks a unified framework for sleep-scoring terminology, definitions, and reporting. Laboratories vary in recording modalities, temporal resolution, staging criteria, and analytical approaches, reflecting both historical practices and the diverse experimental questions addressed using rodent models. Ongoing efforts to harmonize and standardize rodent sleep methodologies are therefore important for improving rigor, reproducibility, and cross-study comparison. However, methodological harmonization also requires a shared vocabulary and clear operational definitions to understand how scoring and analytical approaches are implemented and how methodological choices influence reported outcomes. In this Perspective, we examine variability surrounding fundamental constructs in rodent sleep analysis, including epochs, bouts, segments, fragmentation, and consolidation. We illustrate how choices such as epoch duration and bout initiation, continuation, and termination criteria can alter sleep-stage assignment, bout number and duration, transition frequency, and ultimately the apparent fragmentation or consolidation of sleep. We further distinguish epochs, defined as temporal units receiving vigilance-state assignments, from segments used for signal processing, feature extraction, or data aggregation, and emphasize the importance of defining the specific metrics used to characterize fragmentation and consolidation. Complementing broader efforts to harmonize rodent sleep methodologies, we propose consistent terminology, explicit operational definitions, and minimum reporting practices that make methodological and analytical decisions transparent across recording and scoring approaches. Together, methodological harmonization and a shared vocabulary can strengthen reproducibility, facilitate meaningful cross-study comparison and meta-analysis, and improve translation across experimental models and to human sleep research.

ai.reason: Directly tackles standardization of rodent sleep scoring, epoch/bout definitions, and reproducibility—highly relevant to animal sleep experiments and cross-study harmonization.
ai.summary: This perspective examines variability in rodent sleep-scoring nomenclature, definitions, and methodologies, illustrating how choices such as epoch duration and bout criteria alter sleep-stage assignment and apparent fragmentation/consolidation. It proposes consistent terminology, explicit operational definitions, and minimum reporting practices to improve reproducibility and cross-study comparison.

papers.title: MM-SleepNet: An Automatic Sleep Staging Network Based on Modal Re-Weighting and Mamba.
papers.abstract: Sleep staging is the key step in sleep quality assessment and sleep disorder diagnosis. In clinical practice, doctors usually use polysomnography (PSG) to stage sleep. PSG contains physiological signals such as electroencephalography (EEG) and electrooculography (EOG) and is divided into continuous epochs of fixed duration. In order to achieve more efficient and accurate automatic interpretation of PSG, this paper proposes MM-SleepNet, an automatic sleep staging network based on modal re-weighting and Mamba. MM-SleepNet divides each epoch into several overlapping patches and uses a newly designed patch feature extractor to extract the features of each patch, in order to solve the problem of key waveforms in the patch being obscured by non-key waveforms throughout the epoch. Afterward, MM-SleepNet calculates the importance of different signals on patches at the same time point through a dynamic re-weighting module. MM-SleepNet uses a bidirectional Mamba encoder that considers positional encoding to learn contextual information across epochs to adapt to the transition patterns between sleep stages. The experimental results on the Sleep-EDF and ISRUC datasets show that the proposed MM-SleepNet outperforms state-of-the-art methods. In addition, ablation experiments have demonstrated the effectiveness of various modules in MM-SleepNet.

ai.summary: The paper proposes MM-SleepNet, an automatic sleep staging network using modal re-weighting and a bidirectional Mamba encoder to learn contextual information across epochs. On Sleep-EDF and ISRUC datasets, MM-SleepNet outperformed state-of-the-art methods, and ablation experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of its modules.

papers.title: Repeated self-administered EEG recordings enable longitudinal measurement of brain activity at home
papers.abstract: Mobile electroencephalography (EEG) offers new opportunities to investigate brain activity outside the laboratory, but the quality and reliability of self-administered recordings remain important concerns. Here, we evaluated whether repeated at-home recordings using a four-channel consumer EEG device could provide meaningful electrophysiological measurements and characterized the stability of these measures across sessions. Five participants completed repeated recordings across multiple days, including resting-state measurements and an auditory oddball task performed with and without concurrent cognitive load. The recordings captured established spectral signatures of physiological state and task demands, including increased alpha activity during eye closure and changes in theta activity associated with cognitive load. Auditory stimulation elicited clear event-related responses, while exploratory multivariate decoding distinguished standard from target tones across recording sessions. Measurement stability varied across electrophysiological features, and aggregating repeated sessions improved the consistency of individual-level estimates. For example, split-half reliability of the auditory N1-like response increased from r = .22 with one session to r = .76 with seven sessions per half. By demonstrating the feasibility of repeated self-administered EEG measurements, this study provides a step toward investigating how brain activity varies both between individuals and within individuals over time in everyday environments.

ai.summary: Five participants completed repeated self-administered four-channel consumer EEG recordings at home during rest and an auditory oddball task with and without cognitive load, capturing alpha increases with eye closure, load-related theta changes, and clear event-related responses. Aggregating sessions improved reliability, with split-half reliability of the N1-like response rising from r = .22 for one session to r = .76 for seven sessions per half.

papers.title: EEG-Based Recognition of Self-Imagined Emotions Using Multi-Domain Features and Subject-Specific Calibration.
papers.abstract: Self-imagined emotional imagery, in which individuals internally generate emotional states without external induction, plays a key role in shaping affective brain-computer interface (BCI) systems. Robust generalization across individuals is challenging due to significant variability in EEG patterns. This study evaluates a multi-domain electroencephalography (EEG) decoding framework for self-imagined emotion recognition, integrating time-frequency features, functional connectivity, effective connectivity, and subject-specific calibration. EEG data were collected from 38 participants and categorized into four emotional conditions using the valence-arousal model. Time-frequency features were extracted using the wavelet transform; functional connectivity was assessed using the phase locking value (PLV) and Pearson's correlation; and effective connectivity was estimated using Granger causality. For comparison, a two-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN) based on the continuous wavelet transform was implemented. Under pooled sample-wise cross-validation, PLV-based features combined with a support vector machine (SVM) achieved 97.0% accuracy, while the CNN reached 94.75%. Under leave-one-subject-out evaluation, accuracy declined to approximately 25-30%, indicating limited generalization to unseen participants. With subject-specific calibration using 75% of the target participant's data, the SVM achieved 95.0% accuracy. The results support the recognition of four emotional conditions under the evaluated protocol when data from the target participant are available. However, cross-subject generalizability remains a significant limitation. As the study was conducted under controlled experimental conditions, further research involving independent populations and experimental settings is necessary to evaluate the framework's robustness and applicability.

ai.reason: Multi-domain time-frequency features with subject-specific calibration and SVM generalize well; calibration-from-small-labeled-data approach is directly transferable, though emotion-BCI application is adjacent.
ai.summary: The study evaluated a multi-domain EEG decoding framework for self-imagined emotion recognition using time-frequency features, functional and effective connectivity, and subject-specific calibration in 38 participants. PLV-based features with SVM achieved 97.0% accuracy under pooled cross-validation but only ~25–30% under leave-one-subject-out, while subject-specific calibration using 75% of target data restored accuracy to 95.0%.

papers.title: Hemodynamic spectral signatures across vigilance states: a whole-night EEG/fNIRS investigation.
papers.abstract: Sleep is accompanied by coordinated changes in neuronal activity and cerebral hemodynamics. However, cortical hemodynamic signatures across sleep stages remain poorly characterized, partly because most human electroencephalography (EEG)/functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies are limited in duration, rarely capture deep or Rapid-Eye-Movement (REM) sleep, have low sampling rate, or rely on a sleep-deprivation paradigm, which limits the generalizability of findings. Here, we combined whole-night polysomnography, EEG and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) in healthy young adults, as a bedside technology to monitor cortical hemodynamic fluctuations. We recorded fNIRS using an optimal, personalized, locally dense bilateral frontoparietal montage, alongside peripheral physiology recordings (respiration, photoplethysmography, mean arterial pressure). We computed oscillatory components of oxy- and deoxyhemoglobin (HbO-HbR) spectra across sleep stages using wavelet-based time-frequency analysis. Additionally, we analyzed within the same regions an independent sleep EEG-fMRI dataset (no REM recorded). Our results are suggesting that across frontal and parietal regions, slow-frequency (0.002-0.1Hz) power increased during N1 sleep in HbO and then progressively attenuated across N2 and N3 sleep, in HbO, HbR, and fMRI. REM showed a re-emergence of very-low-frequency power (<0.01Hz) in HbO and HbR. Higher-frequency oscillations (0.15-0.5Hz; overlapping respiratory-band) were selectively enhanced during NREM sleep (largest increase during N3) and returned toward wake-like levels during REM in frontal regions, with regional differences. Peripheral signals captured systemic physiology oscillations but did not reproduce the cortical stage-specific patterns. Together, our findings provide a cortical characterization of sleep-stage hemodynamic organizations that can serve as a reference for future mechanistic and clinical sleep studies.

ai.reason: Whole-night vigilance-state spectral analysis with wavelet time-frequency methods; relevant to sleep staging and spectral analysis, though multimodal hemodynamics less directly transferable to rodent EEG.
ai.summary: Using whole-night EEG and fNIRS in healthy young adults, the study characterized cortical hemodynamic spectral signatures across vigilance states, showing slow-frequency (0.002–0.1 Hz) power increased in N1 and attenuated across N2/N3, while very-low-frequency (<0.01 Hz) power re-emerged in REM. Higher-frequency oscillations (0.15–0.5 Hz) were enhanced during NREM sleep and returned toward wake-like levels in REM.

papers.title: Simulation-based neural dynamics of stress-related negative cognitive bias in depressive symptoms: a dynamical EEG/ERP framework.
papers.abstract: This simulation-based computational study develops a non-linear state-space framework for stress-related negative cognitive bias and multivariate EEG/ERP observations. A three-state model represents negative bias, cognitive control, and arousal, while symptom load and normalized model stress input reshape a quartic bias potential. N2, P3, late positive potential, frontal theta, frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA), and frontoparietal phase locking provide complementary observation channels. Additional checks distinguish the non-linear benchmark from additive and interaction-only competing generators, examine equilibria of the full coupled system, and perturb the observation model. We establish bounded stochastic dynamics, a conditional scalar multistability boundary, stable-branch stress sensitivity, and a sufficient local state-observability condition. A seeded benchmark with 180 simulated participants yields model-implied stress-by-symptom slopes of 66.83 ms for response time, 1.12 μV for LPP, 0.775 dB for frontal theta, 0.133 for FAA, and 0.0769 for frontoparietal PLV. Under a non-linear generating process, mean held-out RMSE was 0.060 for the pre-specified quartic candidate vs. 0.436 for the interaction-only candidate. State-reconstruction RMSE increased from 0.152 under the nominal loading matrix to 0.232 under 15% loading perturbations. These results demonstrate implementation consistency and characterize model sensitivity; they are not clinical effect estimates or evidence of empirical parameter identifiability.

ai.reason: Non-linear state-space and dynamical-systems framework for multivariate EEG, directly aligned with the researcher's interest in state-space and dynamical modeling despite clinical depression framing.
ai.summary: Developed a simulation-based nonlinear state-space framework with three states (negative bias, cognitive control, arousal) linking stress-related negative cognitive bias to EEG/ERP measures, testing it on 180 simulated participants. The pre-specified quartic model achieved mean held-out RMSE 0.060 versus 0.436 for an interaction-only candidate, and state-reconstruction RMSE rose from 0.152 to 0.232 under 15% loading perturbations; these are model-sensitivity results, not clinical effect estimates.

papers.title: Theoretical analysis of transfer learning for temporally dependent observations.
papers.abstract: Transfer learning has become increasingly important in recent years as it enables models to quickly adapt to new tasks, environments and data sets. It can improve the accuracy of machine learning models and reduce the training time required for them. However, theoretical foundation of transfer learning algorithms is rather scarce, particularly for time series models. In this work, we focus on high-dimensional vector autoregressive models and provide a two-step procedure to conduct transfer learning utilizing auxiliary data sets followed by constructing confidence intervals for model parameters in the high-dimensional regime. Further, a new method to select informative sets from auxiliary sets is introduced. Finally, two debiasing techniques are developed to perform inference for model parameters. Theoretical properties of all proposed algorithms are established under mild conditions which allow for heavy-tailed distributions and dependence among auxiliary and target data sets. Given certain level of similarity between the informative models and the target model, it is shown that the proposed algorithm achieves the minimax rate. Lastly, the empirical performance of proposed methods is tested through analyzing both simulated data as well as an EEG data set.

papers.title: A Lightweight Hybrid-Attention Conformer for Affective State Recognition from Wearable EEG.
papers.abstract: Recognizing affective states from electroencephalography (EEG) is a core task in affective computing, with applications in mental health monitoring and public safety. Most existing approaches rely on handcrafted features or image-based transformations of EEG, while transformer models capture global context at high computational cost. This study proposes KimiFormer, an end-to-end hybrid-attention Conformer that classifies raw EEG directly. A hierarchical Spatio-Temporal Stemming (STS) module tokenizes the multichannel signal and learns inter-electrode relationships. Stacked Conformer blocks combine linear and full attention in a 3:1 ratio, reducing computational cost while preserving long-range modeling. The model was evaluated on the public EEG Violence Dataset, recorded with a 14-channel wearable headset from 14 participants viewing violent and neutral videos. Under record-wise leave-one-record-out cross-validation with nested selection of the training hyperparameters, KimiFormer achieved 95.5% accuracy (97.0% under 10-fold cross-validation). On the external DREAMER dataset, its subject-independent performance remained close to chance (balanced accuracy 52.7% for valence and 50.2% for arousal), as did that of two established raw-EEG models. Ablation showed the STS module to be essential (65% accuracy without it). With 3.2 M parameters, 1.51 GFLOPs and an inference latency of 15.64 ms per sample, KimiFormer is suited to real-time, on-device processing of low-channel wearable EEG.

ai.reason: Proposes computationally reduced Conformer for raw EEG affective recognition; lightweight attention design is transferable, though weak subject-independent generalization and emotion focus limit it.
ai.summary: The paper introduces KimiFormer, a lightweight hybrid-attention Conformer that classifies raw wearable EEG for affective state recognition, using a spatio-temporal stemming module and stacked Conformer blocks with linear/full attention. It achieved 95.5% accuracy on the EEG Violence Dataset but near-chance subject-independent performance on DREAMER (balanced accuracy 52.7% valence, 50.2% arousal), with 3.2M parameters and 15.64 ms inference latency.

papers.title: EEG Biomarkers for Stress Detection: A Comparative Analysis of Hjorth Parameters, Spectral and Fractal-Dimension Measures.
papers.abstract: EEG-based stress detection is increasingly relevant for intelligent sensing and human-computer interaction, particularly for systems that aim to adapt to users' changing cognitive and affective states. While conventional EEG-based stress detection approaches mainly rely on spectral band-power features, fractal-dimension measures and Hjorth parameters may provide additional information about underlying brain dynamics. However, their relative contribution, spatial distribution, and frequency-band dependence remain insufficiently understood. In this study, pre-recorded EEG data from a stress-inducing experiment were analyzed using statistical feature pre-selection and multiple machine-learning classifiers. The contribution of different EEG features was evaluated across participants, while scalp topographical maps were used to characterize the spatial distribution of informative features. The results identify Hjorth activity, frontal β asymmetry, and the γ/θ ratio as among the most frequently selected features in the ANOVA-based feature-selection analysis. Combined feature-space configurations including Hjorth parameters and fractal-dimension measures achieved higher classification performance than the conventional-feature reference configuration. These findings provide further insight into the spatial and frequency-specific characteristics of EEG features associated with the investigated stress-inducing cognitive task and demonstrate the value of combining conventional spectral features with Hjorth parameters and fractal-dimension measures for physiological-state sensing. The proposed approach may support the development of computationally efficient EEG-based monitoring of stress-related cognitive states for intelligent and adaptive human-computer interaction, including neuroadaptive and context-aware systems.

ai.reason: Compares Hjorth parameters, spectral, and fractal-dimension features for state detection; efficient interpretable feature work transferable to vigilance/state classification.
ai.summary: Compared Hjorth parameters, fractal-dimension measures, and conventional spectral band-power features for EEG-based stress detection using ANOVA-based feature selection and multiple machine-learning classifiers on pre-recorded stress-experiment data. Hjorth activity, frontal β asymmetry, and the γ/θ ratio were among the most frequently selected features, and combined feature spaces including Hjorth parameters and fractal dimensions outperformed the conventional spectral-feature reference configuration.

papers.title: Sequential syntax of EEG microstates captures the temporal dynamics of inhibitory control.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalogram (EEG) microstates are successive global brain states whose temporal organization may reflect cognitive dynamics that conventional summary statistics do not capture. We applied a sequence-based framework, combining conditional successor analysis with multiple sequence alignment adapted from genomics, to microstate sequences recorded during a Go/NoGo task in 30 healthy adults. Generalized estimating equations showed no condition-level differences in standard microstate metrics. Conditional successor analysis identified three motifs enriched in the NoGo-early window (100-500 ms): A-C-D (p FDR = 0.013), B-A-D (p FDR = 0.029), and E-A-D (p FDR = 0.040), all passing through microstate A and ending in microstate D, consistent with fronto-central engagement. Multiple sequence alignment showed non-random temporal organization in all conditions (all z > 11.5 and p < 0.001). These results support sequence syntax as a framework for linking millisecond-scale brain dynamics to cognitive function.

ai.reason: Sequence-based microstate framework with alignment methods, an interpretable and fairly generalizable time-dynamics approach; adjacency to state-modeling interests but cognitive-task specific.
ai.summary: Applied a sequence-based framework combining conditional successor analysis with multiple sequence alignment to EEG microstate sequences from 30 healthy adults during a Go/NoGo task. Conditional successor analysis identified three NoGo-early motifs (A-C-D, B-A-D, E-A-D) passing through microstate A and ending in D, while sequence alignment showed non-random temporal organization across all conditions.

papers.title: Automatic classification of seizure adequacy in electroconvulsive therapy: A proof-of-concept study
papers.abstract: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is the most effective treatment of a range of severe mental dis-orders and is annually given to more than a million patients worldwide. Dosing of the electrical charge is critical for efficacy and side-effect burden; however, it is currently based on manual assessment of seizure quality and exhibits substantial clinical heterogeneity. Here, we collected 1,000 ECT session electroencephalograms (EEG) from 130 individual ECT patients and made an expert-level classification of the EEGs into actionable seizure quality categories (null-response [0], threshold [T], and adequate [A]). We then trained a range of machine learning algorithms on the raw EEG data to classify the EEGs into these categories and tested for classi-fication accuracy. The highest performing algorithm was able to classify the seizures with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curves of >0.9 for both the 0 vs. T and the T vs. A categories corresponding to excellent discrimination. In contrast, the accuracy of predicting seizure quality in subsequent treatments was only moderate. The addition of clinical variables to the models, such as demographics, anesthesia and anticonvulsant exposure, did not improve model performance. These results provide proof-of-concept of machine learning classification of seizure adequacy in ECT based on raw EEG data. The findings could pave the way for the de-velopment of more objective and personalized decision-support tools in ECT.

Adding clinical variables did not improve performance.

papers.title: Effects of Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring During Polysomnography on Sleep Indices and EEG Power.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) may disturb sleep during polysomnography (PSG), and the first-night effect (FNE) can complicate interpretation. We evaluated changes associated with ABPM and FNE across whole nights and individual measurements. Methods: This secondary analysis included 72 nominally healthy adults in a balanced two-night crossover, with ABPM on one randomly assigned night. Linear mixed-effects models estimated associations with PSG-derived sleep indices, a composite sleep quality index (SQI), and relative electroencephalographic (EEG) power. Analyses of individual measurements summarized EEG changes, sleep-stage transitions, and automated arousal detections. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) adjustment was applied within defined analysis families. Results: FNE and ABPM were associated with lower SQI (β = -0.049 and -0.051, respectively; both BH-adjusted p = 0.028). FNE was associated with altered sleep continuity and architecture, whereas ABPM was associated with higher light-sleep and lower N3-sleep percentages and higher whole-night relative theta power. In the Night 2 paired analysis, relative delta power was lower and relative alpha, beta, and gamma power were higher during ABPM than before ABPM (all BH-adjusted p < 0.01); the theta difference did not reach significance (BH-adjusted p = 0.0632). Of 655 eligible ABPM measurements beginning during sleep, 395 (60.3%) contained at least one arousal detection within the 2 min measurement window. Conclusions: These detections indicate temporal co-occurrence and do not establish that cuff inflation caused arousal. Concurrent ABPM and study-night order should be considered when interpreting PSG. An adaptation PSG night may be considered when feasible, as may cuffless blood pressure monitoring once its accuracy has been established for the intended setting.

Both ABPM and first-night effect were associated with lower composite sleep quality index, ABPM with higher light-sleep and lower N3 percentages and higher relative theta power, and 60.3% of in-sleep ABPM measurements contained at least one arousal detection within the 2-min window.

papers.title: Distinct contemplative traditions share a common EEG complexity signature
papers.abstract: Meditation encompasses diverse practices that train attention inward, unlike externally oriented task states. Which brain-activity features are shared across contemplative practices, which accompany long-term training, and which are tradition-specific remains unclear. We leveraged electroencephalography data from 226 participants: advanced meditators of four contemplative traditions and non-meditating controls. We developed a neurodynamic profiling approach spanning 21 features across four feature families: oscillatory, aperiodic, complexity and timescale. Using extensive machine learning, we found that meditation and task states were reliably separable, driven by a large, uniform drop in complexity during meditation. Meditators differed from controls primarily in timescale dynamics. Traditions exhibited distinct signatures in all feature families except complexity, and meditators neurodynamic profiles identified the contemplative tradition they practiced. A classifier trained on three traditions could still detect meditation in the fourth, regardless of which tradition was left out, relying mainly on complexity features. Diverse contemplative techniques therefore converge on a shared neurodynamic signature - reduced complexity during meditation relative to an external task, that generalizes across traditions. This shared signature coexists with tradition-specific profiles in oscillatory, aperiodic, and timescale features.

Meditation was reliably separable from task states via a large uniform drop in complexity, while meditators differed from controls mainly in timescale dynamics, and a classifier trained on three traditions detected meditation in the held-out fourth, relying mainly on complexity features.

papers.title: Reproducible EEG-BCI Experiments: Frame-Confirmed Timing and Physical SSVEP Validation.
papers.abstract: Reproducible EEG-based brain-computer interface (BCI) experiments require traceability from the configured protocol through runtime execution to acquisition context and, where relevant, the physical stimulus delivered to the participant. This study presents and evaluates a workflow that links machine-readable SSVEP protocols, deterministic session planning, frame-confirmed events, raw acquisition provenance, post-session integrity checks, and independent photoresistor-based display validation. The contribution is not a new acquisition platform or timing sensor, but the integration of these evidence layers into a single auditable experimental chain and the empirical assessment of their consistency. All 61 automated tests passed for the frozen software release. Three optical sweeps covering 8-15 Hz yielded 48 valid measurements, all within the predefined ±0.25 Hz criterion. The mean absolute error was 0.0345 Hz, and the maximum was 0.0668 Hz. In a separate 12.75 Hz rendering-load experiment, all 12 measurements also passed, with mean absolute errors of 0.0170 Hz for a single stimulus and 0.0154 Hz with three simultaneous distractors. Local optical pulse-width anomalies were, nevertheless, observed, particularly at 13-14 Hz and in two multi-stimulus repetitions, showing that dominant-frequency agreement and local timing regularity are distinct validation properties. Formal empirical validation targeted software and session integrity and physical display output; it did not quantify end-to-end event-to-EEG latency through the OpenBCI transport path. The results support a more explicit separation of configured intent, runtime timing evidence, acquisition provenance, and physical stimulus verification in reproducible EEG-BCI experimentation.

ai.summary: Presented and evaluated an auditable EEG-BCI experimental workflow integrating machine-readable SSVEP protocols, deterministic session planning, frame-confirmed events, acquisition provenance, integrity checks, and photoresistor-based display validation. All 61 automated tests passed; 48 of 48 optical sweep measurements (8-15 Hz) fell within ±0.25 Hz (mean absolute error 0.0345 Hz, max 0.0668 Hz), though local optical pulse-width anomalies were observed at 13-14 Hz and in two multi-stimulus repetitions.

papers.title: Self-Organized Explainable Symbolic EEG Feature Engineering Using Directed Lobish and Previous-Next Pattern: A Proof-of-Concept Study on Dementia Classification.
papers.abstract: Objective: Dementia is a prevalent neurological disorder, and accurate detection is essential for timely intervention. This study aims to design an interpretable symbolic feature engineering framework for EEG-based dementia classification and to examine how its performance depends on the validation protocol. Methods: We used a publicly available EEG dementia dataset including Alzheimer's disease (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FD), and healthy controls. A self-organized explainable feature engineering (SOXFE) model was introduced with five phases: (i) feature extraction using Bipartite Channel Transformer (BCT) and Previous-Next Pattern (PNPat), (ii) feature selection via cumulative weight-based iterative neighborhood component analysis (CWINCA), (iii) explainable output generation using Directed Lobish (DLob), (iv) classification through an ensemble tkNN classifier, and (v) information fusion with combinational majority voting (CMV). Performance was evaluated with segment-wise 10-fold cross-validation, leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) cross-validation, and nested participant-grouped 10-fold cross-validation. Results: Segment-wise 10-fold cross-validation, which allowed segments of one participant in both training and test folds, yielded accuracies of 99.12-99.74%. Participant-independent accuracy was substantially lower: 51.19-63.81% for LOSO and 49.00-62.50% for nested participant-grouped validation at the segment level. Participant-level LOSO accuracy equaled the majority-class rate for dementia versus healthy controls (67.05%) and fell below it for AD versus FD (57.63% versus 61.02%). No exact McNemar comparison showed an accuracy advantage over the majority-class baseline. DLob outputs were produced as feature-level visualizations. Conclusions: The findings support the feasibility of interpretable, algorithm-derived symbolic feature representations. They do not establish reproducible disease-related EEG characteristics or clinical diagnostic utility. DLob outputs describe the channel transitions used by the model. Independent cohorts and stronger participant-independent performance are required before clinical application.

ai.reason: Interpretable symbolic feature engineering with careful LOSO/nested validation; explainable features and rigorous protocol are useful, though dementia focus is adjacent.
ai.summary: Designed an interpretable symbolic EEG feature-engineering framework (SOXFE) combining Bipartite Channel Transformer, Previous-Next Pattern, cumulative-weight INCA selection, Directed Lobish explainability, and ensemble tkNN with combinational majority voting for dementia classification. Segment-wise 10-fold cross-validation reached 99.12-99.74% accuracy, but participant-independent accuracy fell to 51.19-63.81% (LOSO) and 49.00-62.50% (nested participant-grouped), with no McNemar advantage over majority-class baselines, so clinical diagnostic utility was not established.

papers.title: BioTWavePat: An EEG-Based Mental Performance Detection Model.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: EEG-based mental performance classification requires participant-separated validation and traceable feature identities. Methods: BioTWavePat-XFE constructs five single-rhythm and 15 signed cross-rhythm channel-rank transition layers, uses four cumulative-weighted selectors and tkNN/IMV classification, and decodes retained identities with Directed Lobish. We compared Protocol A (whole-dataset feature and pooled-test outcome selection), Protocol B (training-fold outcome selection with Protocol A features), and Protocol C (all data-dependent steps restricted to outer training data). STEW and MAT used participant-wise LOSO. TMPD included all 55 participants in 54 identifier groups; two same-class participants sharing an identifier were withheld together. Results: Protocol A segment accuracies were 83.08% (STEW), 93.14% (TMPD), and 91.15% (MAT). Protocol C accuracies were 80.46%, 82.50%, and 74.65%, with balanced accuracies of 80.46%, 75.17%, and 64.15%, respectively. These are the primary estimates without the identified selection leakage under the stated participant-separated validation design. Conclusions: Whole-dataset selection inflated the original estimates, particularly for TMPD and MAT. MAT Protocol C performance was close to majority prediction. Directed Lobish exposes selected feature identities without establishing physiological connectivity, causality or biomarker validity.

ai.reason: Addresses participant-separated validation and traceable feature identities for EEG-based mental performance classification; transferable to sleep staging but focused on mental performance, not sleep.
ai.summary: Introduced BioTWavePat-XFE, an EEG mental performance detection model using signed cross-rhythm channel-rank transition features, cumulative-weighted selectors, and Directed Lobish decoding, evaluated under three data-dependent selection protocols with participant-wise LOSO validation. Under leakage-restricted Protocol C, accuracies fell to 80.46% (STEW), 82.50% (TMPD), and 74.65% (MAT), showing whole-dataset selection inflated original estimates, with MAT near majority-prediction performance.

papers.title: EEG-based Deep Learning Reveals Cortical Sensitivity to Small Changes in Deep Brain Stimulation Parameters.
papers.abstract: Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) is an invasive procedure used to alleviate motor symptoms in Parkinson's Disease (PD) patients. Despite its effectiveness, the impact of DBS on brain activity and the way to optimise stimulation parameters remains unclear. In this study, we aimed to map the sensitivity of cortical neural response to changes in DBS parameters in real-world clinical settings. We recorded in-clinic EEG data from PD patients during their clinical DBS programming sessions, both at rest and during arm movement. A siamese variant of the EEGNet deep learning architecture was trained independently for each patient and parameter combination to determine whether two 1-sec-long EEG segments were recorded under the same or different DBS parameters, yielding 30 independently trained models. Our models achieved an average accuracy of 74% in classifying whether two 1-second EEG segments corresponded to the same or different DBS parameters. Explainability methods were then applied to extract the neural oscillations learned by the models. Ablation studies identified mid-gamma oscillations (55-90Hz) as the key band for classifying these changes. Importantly, that was not driven by 1:2 gamma entrainment. In a sub-group of patients, the theta-alpha oscillations (4-12Hz) also contributed to detecting changes in DBS parameters. We demonstrate that small DBS parameter changes modify cortical activity in a consistent manner that can be detected using shallow convolutional networks on low-density EEG. Our findings suggest that cortical mid-gamma oscillations (55-90Hz) are highly sensitive to small changes in DBS settings. Our approach and findings could be leveraged towards identifying and defining novel digital biomarkers to guide DBS programming and adaptive DBS systems.

papers.title: EEG and hedonic responses to sonic-seasoning soundscapes: a dataset.
papers.abstract: This dataset comprises electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings from 30 adult participants exposed to two contrasting designed soundscapes - a natural, sustainability-conveying "organic jungle" soundscape and a contrasting "deconstruct" soundscape - together with their liking ratings of each soundscape and basic demographic information. The data extend the largely behavioral "sonic-seasoning" literature, which has shown that sound and music systematically shape the sensory and affective evaluation of consumer experiences, by adding a complementary neurophysiological measurement angle. EEG was acquired with a 14-channel consumer-grade EMOTIV EPOC X headset (128 Hz) on a web-based experiment platform that logged synchronized event markers. For each participant the dataset provides: a resting calibration recording (eyes-open and eyes-closed); the EEG recorded during a brief (∼17 s) isolated exposure to each of the two soundscapes; the corresponding liking ratings; the soundscape stimulus audio files; and demographic responses. EEG data are released as recorded, with the manufacturer's per-channel contact-quality and signal-quality indices retained, so that re-users can apply any preprocessing or analytic pipeline. These data are of value to researchers in sonic seasoning and multisensory marketing, affective and consumer neuroscience, and to those developing or benchmarking methods for consumer-grade EEG. The included liking ratings provide a behavioral anchor relating the neural data to the affective character of the soundscapes.

papers.title: Automated Detection of Abnormal Pediatric Electroencephalograms Using Machine Learning: Retrospective Study.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is widely used in medicine as a technique for the assessment of several brain-related pathologies. However, EEG interpretation requires specialized expertise and remains a labor-intensive task, particularly for prolonged recordings in intensive care, where timely expert review is often challenging. The aim of this study is to address this problem by using AI methods to automate EEG interpretation and compare the performance of different modeling approaches. A gradient boosting-based model, inspired by the work of Albaqami et al, was implemented and compared to deep learning (DL)-based models using convolutional neural networks to classify images generated from raw EEG signals. The models were trained and tested on pediatric EEGs acquired at the University Hospital in Essen. The DL model showed higher observed sensitivity (78.3%) and F1-score (80%) compared to the gradient boosting model (sensitivity: 65.2%; F1-score: 73.8%), indicating improved detection of abnormal EEGs. However, the gradient boosting approach achieved higher specificity (93% vs 89.6%), suggesting a stronger ability to recognize normal EEGs. Overall, both methods yielded promising results, with classification accuracies reaching up to 85.3%. Both approaches show potential for automated EEG interpretation. Future improvements, including larger and more diverse datasets, refined DL architectures, and integration of explainable AI techniques, could further enhance performance.

The DL model achieved higher sensitivity (78.3%) and F1-score (80%) while gradient boosting achieved higher specificity (93% vs 89.6%), with overall accuracies up to 85.3%.

papers.title: Temporal evolution of EEG band power at freezing of gait onset in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Although EEG studies have implicated theta-, alpha-, and beta-band activity in freezing of gait (FoG) in Parkinson's disease (PD), most have relied on resting-state comparisons, task contrasts, or connectivity analyses rather than modeling band-power changes around FoG onset. This study investigated the temporal evolution of EEG spectral power around FoG onset during ecological walking. We analyzed a multimodal dataset comprising 10 individuals with PD and FoG during ecological walking. Two hundred and four FoG episodes were analyzed. EEG was recorded from 25 scalp electrodes and time-locked to FoG onset. Relative spectral power was computed for theta, alpha, and beta bands. Channel-wise piecewise linear mixed-effects models evaluated pre-FoG trends, onset-related shifts, and post-onset slope changes. Multiple comparisons were controlled using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR, q < 0.05). Theta power showed no significant pre-FoG trend but increased abruptly at FoG onset at F3 and Fz. Alpha power exhibited a progressive pre-FoG increase at FP1, F3, F8, Fz, and Cz, whereas no onset-related or post-onset alpha effects survived FDR correction. Beta power showed no significant temporal modulation after correction. These findings indicate temporal profiles, with alpha changes preceding FoG and theta changes emerging at onset. FoG onset during ecological walking is associated with dissociable low-frequency EEG dynamics. Frontal and midline alpha increases may characterize a pre-freezing state, whereas abrupt frontal theta increases are associated with the transition into FoG. These patterns represent candidate electrophysiological features that require prospective validation before predictive or biomarker applications can be established.

papers.title: The Case for Low-Friction High-Adherence Passive Sleep-Tracking Devices in Longitudinal Monitoring of Neurodegenerative Disease.
papers.abstract: Digital health technologies are playing an increasingly important role in patient monitoring, able to capture longitudinal data to supplement scheduled episodic evaluations conducted by clinicians. Rapid advances in sensors and data processing algorithms have resulted in some highly sophisticated systems capable of monitoring and tracking numerous symptoms with high levels of sensitivity and specificity. These approaches, however, often require active engagement with the patient, potentially increasing burden in a clinical trial and often resulting in diminishing adherence over time. In the case of slow-progressing neurodegenerative diseases, this may become an obstacle, as often very subtle changes in symptoms are typically monitored over a multi-year period. Accordingly, there is evident interest in passive monitoring solutions which have minimal burden on patients. Smart ring technologies are one such solution, with appealing form factors, low engagement requirements and increasing intervals before device recharging is required. While newer devices are capable of tracking sleep function with increasing levels of accuracy, they are unable to offer the precision afforded by gold standard sleep analysis such as electroencephalography (EEG), polysomnography (PSG) and sleep laboratory protocols. Prompted by a recent study which highlighted the reduced accuracy of consumer-based sleep devices compared with conventional approaches, we posit that the benefits of such devices may offset the constraints of measurement accuracy. Furthermore, any accuracy-adherence trade-offs would be compensated by long-term statistical benefits derived from detecting within-person changes and reducing measurement noise through enhanced sampling frequencies. In this perspective, we highlight their potential utility in tracking Parkinson's disease patients longitudinally, where compromised sleep architectures are associated with multiple symptoms and continuous monitoring could offer myriad patient benefits.

papers.title: Predicting Motor Recovery in the Subacute Phase of Stroke: The Role of Passive Motor Task and Electroencephalogram Brain Networks.
papers.abstract: In stroke rehabilitation, the identification of reliable prognostic factors remains a challenge for effective rehabilitation strategies. This study investigates which motor task has the most predictive utility based on electroencephalogram (EEG) characteristics during the subacute phase of stroke. Data were collected from 10 subacute stroke patients performed different motor tasks (passive, robotic movement; active, voluntary execution; motor imagery [MI]) and a nonmotor task (No-Go) at two time points: T1, approximately 3 weeks after stroke onset, and T2, 2 months after T1. EEG power and network characteristics were extracted for each task, and prognostic models were constructed with nested leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) cross-validation (CV) to avoid information leakage. Our findings show that the passive task model produced the strongest internal predictive performance across all task conditions (root-mean-square error 5.94; nested LOSO CV-R2, 0.91), with ipsilesional/contralesional motor area event-related desynchronization, characteristic path length, and clustering coefficient emerging as consistent prognostic features. The passive task also showed less overactivation and hyperconnectivity in the early subacute phase relative to the active and MI tasks. This performance advantage was replicated across six analytic procedures (2 feature-selection × 3 regression strategies), supporting the robustness of the task comparison within the present dataset. These findings suggest that EEG features obtained during a robot-assisted passive task may provide exploratory prognostic utility for motor recovery prediction in the early subacute phase of stroke.Impact StatementThe passive task may offer a practical approach for assessing neurophysiological markers of recovery potential, supporting the development of more personalized rehabilitation strategies and earlier prognostic evaluation in stroke patients.

Consistent prognostic features were ipsilesional/contralesional motor-area event-related desynchronization, characteristic path length, and clustering coefficient, with less overactivation and hyperconnectivity in the early subacute phase.

papers.title: A Hybrid Deep Learning Model (CNN-GRU) with MRMR for EEG-Based Depression Detection.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a prevalent mental health disorder for which objective and reliable diagnostic approaches remain an active area of research. Electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a promising non-invasive modality for identifying neural activity patterns associated with depression, while advances in deep learning have enabled effective analysis of complex EEG signals. Methods: In this study, we propose a hybrid deep learning framework that integrates convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for spatial feature extraction and gated recurrent units (GRUs) for temporal modeling of EEG signals. The spatial and temporal features extracted by the CNN and GRU components were concatenated into a 120-dimensional representation, after which minimum redundancy maximum relevance (mRMR) feature selection was applied to reduce redundancy and retain the 30 most informative features before classification. The proposed framework was evaluated using the publicly available MODMA EEG dataset, and its performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Results: Across 30 independent simulation runs, the CNN-GRU-mRMR framework achieved a mean classification accuracy of 96.74%, exceeding the performance of the comparison methods evaluated in this study. The model also demonstrated high precision, recall, and F1-score, indicating strong classification performance within the evaluated dataset. Conclusions: These findings suggest that integrating spatial and temporal feature learning with mRMR-based feature selection can improve EEG-based depression classification. Further validation using larger, more diverse, and independent clinical datasets is needed to establish the generalizability of the framework and evaluate its potential utility for objective EEG-based depression assessment.

ai.summary: Proposed a hybrid CNN-GRU deep learning framework with mRMR feature selection for EEG-based depression detection, evaluated on the MODMA dataset. Across 30 simulation runs, it achieved a mean classification accuracy of 96.74%, outperforming the comparison methods.

papers.title: Combined MEG and EEG suggest a limbic source network for the P3.
papers.abstract: The event-related P3 is evoked by most task-relevant or salient stimuli, but its neural sources remain controversial. Here we reevaluate the role of hippocampus, unambiguously demonstrated in intracranial recordings, and retro-splenial cortex as sources of the P3 in magneto- and electroencephalography. Observers detected rare visual targets of a deviant shape and ignored rare non-targets of a deviant color. Source analysis was based on noise-normalized minimum-norm estimates in an individual, MRI-based source space. Critically, the cortical source space was extended to include the cornu ammonis of the hippocampus. Source analysis at the P3 peak showed strong sources in retrosplenial cortex and a weaker source in hippocampus. Activity in left somatosensory cortex was related to the button presses. Subsequent activity was observed in insula and anterior mid-cingulate cortex. Further simulation studies explored the spread of these sources and the plausibility of their combination to explain the data, and demonstrate that the combination of magneto- and electroencephalography increased the specificity of the source estimate. Overall, these data support an interpretation of the P3 as physiological indicator of activity in the limbic system for target and distractor stimuli.

At the P3 peak, source analysis showed strong retrosplenial cortex and weaker hippocampal sources, with later insula and anterior mid-cingulate activity, supporting a limbic-system interpretation of the P3; simulations indicated combined MEG/EEG improved source specificity.

papers.title: Explainable Rhythm-Resolved EEG for Retrospective Comparison of Psychiatric-Service Adults with Recorded Violent Offences and Non-Clinical Controls.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: This study examines whether rhythm-resolved EEG features separate two retrospective groups and whether those features can be traced to explicit rhythms and sensors. The groups are psychiatric-service adults with recorded violent offences and non-clinical controls; the design does not compare offenders with non-offenders. Methods: We analysed 2554 non-overlapping 15 s EEG epochs from 95 adults (51 controls; 44 recorded-offence participants). RhythmFluxPat generated 9216 rank-transition features. CWImRMR selected 352 features with full-cohort labels, and classifier selection was nested within 95 participant-held-out leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) folds. Results: Classifier-nested tkNN classified 2392/2554 epochs (93.66%) and 93/95 participants (97.89%), and an independent check reproduced both confusion matrices. A nested support-vector machine (SVM) gave similar values (94.71% of epochs; 93/95 participants). In the comparative evaluation of four feature selectors, CWImRMR remained the best branch (93.85%), and a 44-feature subset reached 91.11%. DRLobish linked the selected features to delta and beta-to-gamma routes in the recorded-offence-assigned panel and to theta and alpha-to-theta routes in the control-assigned panel. Conclusions: RhythmFluxPat provides traceable rank-persistence and rank-exchange coordinates. The reported accuracies are optimistic internal estimates. Fully nested replication with matched psychiatric controls is required before any claim of generalisation or biomarker validity.

ai.summary: Applied rhythm-resolved rank-transition EEG features (RhythmFluxPat) with an explainable classifier to retrospectively separate psychiatric-service adults with recorded violent offences from non-clinical controls. A nested tkNN classified 93/95 participants (97.89%), with DRLobish linking features to delta and beta-to-gamma versus theta and alpha-to-theta rhythm routes, while the authors caution these are optimistic internal estimates.

papers.title: Quantum-Kernel Learning for Subject-Independent EEG Emotion Recognition with Spectral-Connectivity Features.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based emotion recognition remains challenging under subject-independent evaluation because of substantial inter-subject variability. This study investigates the feasibility of state-fidelity-based quantum-kernel learning for subject-independent valence and arousal recognition using differential entropy (DE) and phase-locking value (PLV) features. Using the DEAP dataset, DE and PLV features were extracted and evaluated individually and in combination, with subject-wise normalization and F-score feature selection applied within the evaluation framework. Six features were retained for valence and eight for arousal. The selected features were encoded using a Qiskit ZFeatureMap, and the fidelity-based quantum kernel was evaluated through statevector simulation on a classical computer. Quantum-kernel, Linear, and RBF SVMs were compared using nested participant-grouped cross-validation across DE, PLV, and DE-PLV feature representations. For valence, the quantum-kernel SVM using DE features achieved the highest mean balanced accuracy of 59.18%. For arousal, the Linear SVM using DE features achieved the highest mean balanced accuracy of 54.16%. Overall, the three classifiers showed comparable performance across the evaluated feature representations. These results support the feasibility of state-fidelity-based quantum similarity for subject-independent EEG emotion recognition.

ai.summary: Investigated state-fidelity-based quantum-kernel SVM learning for subject-independent EEG valence and arousal recognition using differential entropy and phase-locking value features from the DEAP dataset. Quantum-kernel SVM reached the highest mean balanced accuracy of 59.18% for valence, while Linear SVM with DE features led arousal at 54.16%, with comparable overall performance across classifiers.

papers.title: Cortical Network Alterations and Treatment-Induced Reorganization in Panic Disorder: A Longitudinal High-Density EEG Study.
papers.abstract: Although neuroimaging has identified network abnormalities in panic disorder (PD), the rapid and transient nature of panic symptoms highlights the need for methods with high temporal resolution. This study used high-density electroencephalography (EEG) to investigate cortical network alterations in PD and explore their potential as translational biomarkers. This longitudinal study enrolled 52 drug-naïve PD patients and 43 healthy controls. High-density (128-channel) resting-state EEG was collected from both groups at baseline, with repeat assessments performed in PD patients after 6 weeks of venlafaxine treatment. Source-level functional connectivity and network topology were analyzed to characterize cortical network features. Support vector machine (SVM) was used to evaluate the discriminative potential of baseline network features. At baseline, PD patients showed frequency-specific network disruptions, with enhanced connectivity within and between the default mode network, frontoparietal network, and dorsal attention network in the α band, but reduced connectivity across multiple networks in the θ and δ bands. Graph theory analysis revealed decreased global efficiency and increased characteristic path length in the α and δ bands. The SVM classifier achieved 86.32% accuracy in distinguishing PD patients from controls. Following treatment, clinical improvement was accompanied by network reorganization, including increased global efficiency and small-worldness in the α band, and enhanced fronto-temporal connectivity in the δ band. Exploratory brain-behavior associations did not survive FDR correction. PD is characterized by frequency-specific cortical network disruptions that show dynamic reorganization following treatment. These findings highlight the potential of EEG-derived network features as candidate markers for PD identification and treatment monitoring.

papers.title: Correlation and Agreement Between Bispectral Index Monitoring and Quantitative EEG in Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage.
papers.abstract: Delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) is a major cause of poor outcome after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH). Continuous EEG can predict DCI but is resource intensive. Processed EEG monitors such as the bispectral index (BIS) are simpler, yet their relationship with quantitative EEG (qEEG) parameters remains unclear. We evaluated the correlation and agreement between BIS and qEEG in aSAH. Single-center prospective study of adults with aSAH who underwent two 30-min routine EEG recordings with simultaneous bilateral BIS monitoring (within 72 h of admission and on days 4-7). qEEG parameters were extracted from frontal channels adjacent to the BIS sensor and from full-montage EEG recordings. Prespecified comparisons included BIS total power (BIS-tpw), spectral edge frequency (BIS-sef), and BIS value (BIS-v) with corresponding qEEG measures. Correlation and agreement were assessed using correlation coefficients, intraclass correlation, concordance analysis, regression methods, and Bland-Altman approaches. Exploratory analyses evaluated the DCI interaction in BIS-qEEG associations and concordance for DCI detection. Sixty-four patients contributed 248 paired BIS-qEEG observations. Prespecified parameter pairs showed moderate-to-strong correlations (ρ > 0.6), particularly between BIS-tpw and qEEG power measures and between BIS-sef and qEEG-sef. Agreement analyses were fair to good for BIS-tpw and BIS-sef [absolute intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) up to ~0.75; consistency ICCs ≥ 0.80]. In contrast, BIS-v showed weak correlations, poor agreement, and substantial between-patient variability. Associations were strongest with frontal qEEG parameters, whereas correlations with full-montage qEEG measures were moderate. DCI was associated with consistent BIS-qEEG differences and fair-to-good concordance. BIS-derived parameters, particularly BIS-tpw and BIS-sef, were associated with qEEG measures of spectral power and frequency in aSAH. In contrast, BIS-v showed weaker and less reliable relationships with qEEG metrics. BIS monitoring may provide complementary bedside electrophysiological trends when continuous EEG is unavailable but should not be considered interchangeable with qEEG.

papers.title: Electrophysiology of multisite direct electrical stimulation in the human brain
papers.abstract: Human cognition and neurological disorders reflect properties of distributed networks, yet how best to engage these networks therapeutically remains unknown. Multisite stimulation is a principled strategy for engaging brain networks, but a key translational barrier is understanding how a network combines concurrent inputs from multiple nodes. Here, we investigated the electrophysiology of simultaneous multisite direct electrical stimulation in 20 participants implanted with stereo-EEG electrodes. Synchronized dual-site stimulation engaged a larger effective network than single-site stimulation. Linear superposition explained most responses, but distinct nonlinear responses were also observed. Sublinear responses, consistent with saturation, occurred proximal to stimulation sites, while supralinear responses arose in network-connected sites during the response's late component. Moreover, low-intensity dual-site stimulation matched or exceeded single-site stimulation at higher intensities. These principles extended to three-site stimulation. These findings systematically characterize how responses to simultaneous multisite stimulation interact in the human brain, a foundational step towards principled, network-guided neurostimulation therapies.

papers.title: Interpersonal alignment in infra-slow EEG rhythms and bodily signals anticipates mutual recognition
papers.abstract: Across multiple timescales, neural rhythms coordinate cognitive and physiological processes. Slower rhythms are increasingly recognised as the scale at which autonomic and interoceptive processes are folded into ongoing cognition, a brain&body view of allostatic regulation that is particularly relevant to social interaction. Examining these slow components of the electroencephalogram (EEG) during real-time interaction remains challenging. Here, we recorded infra-slow EEG alongside respiratory, cardiac and skin conductance signals during the perceptual crossing experiment, a social interaction and EEG hyperscanning paradigm. We assessed interpersonal alignment by contrasting trials in which dyads achieved mutual recognition with trials in which they did not, which separates genuine social alignment or recognition from a shared anticipatory context. Dyads achieving mutual recognition showed enhanced inter-participant alignment of 0.1 Hz infra-slow EEG power relative to those that did not, after accounting for the premovement motor potential. Alignment also differed between these trials in respiratory depth, the cardiac vagal index and skin conductance. These findings suggest that infra-slow EEG rhythms around 0.1 Hz may provide a temporal scaffold for the interpersonal coordination of brain and body, and could serve as markers for investigating the coupled processes underlying shared understanding and mutual recognition.

Mutual recognition trials showed enhanced inter-participant alignment of 0.1 Hz infra-slow EEG power and differences in respiratory depth, cardiac vagal index and skin conductance, suggesting infra-slow rhythms as a temporal scaffold for interpersonal brain-body coordination.

papers.title: Brain-computer interfaces for neurodegenerative diseases: A comprehensive review of closed-loop systems from diagnosis to neural rehabilitation.
papers.abstract: Brain-computer interface (BCI) technology serves as an important bridge between the nervous system and external devices and has shown considerable promise for the diagnosis and treatment of neurodegenerative diseases, whose global burden continues to increase: in 2021, more than 57 million people were living with dementia worldwide, with Alzheimer's disease (AD) accounting for approximately 60-70% of cases, while an estimated 11.77 million people were living with Parkinson's disease (PD) in 2021, according to the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021. This growing disease burden, together with the progressive loss of cognitive, motor, and communicative functions, highlights the need for more precise approaches to early detection, functional assistance, and individualized intervention. Conventional diagnostic and therapeutic approaches remain poorly suited to early detection and timely intervention. This paper analyzes the development of BCI technology, from the first detection of electroencephalogram (EEG) signals to the parallel development of invasive and non-invasive systems, and outlines the basic principles of signal acquisition, processing, and decoding, together with the relative advantages and limitations of different approaches. It then focuses on the use of BCI in Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), covering early diagnosis, functional reconstruction, and neuromodulation. The article also discusses the difficulties encountered by BCI technology in terms of technological realization, clinical translation, and ethical considerations, as well as several future research directions, including multimodal fusion, adaptive algorithms, closed-loop control systems, and personalized treatment so as to drive the applications of BCI in precision medicine and in neurological diseases.

papers.title: Investigation of Brain Performance in the Schizophrenia Spectrum Using EEG with Mental and Temporal Effort.
papers.abstract: Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorder, widely known as causing behavioral changes, deprives many professionals-who remain capable of working-their jobs. This study aimed to investigate the use of electroencephalography exam (EEG) combined with standardized mental effort sequence as a complementary tool for clinical diagnosis and to monitor the treatment response in individuals with schizophrenia and those who want to return to professional activities. EEG recordings were acquired before (IR_Initial Register) and after (FR_Final Register) the completion of a set of timed mental effort tasks in a group of 25 clinically stable individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia with positive symptoms and an 11-member healthy volunteer control group. Data from both groups were compared using temporal and spectral descriptors, and the results were analyzed statistically. The results revealed that, in the FR phase, the Vtotal parameter for the schizophrenia group was 7.89% lower, and the frequency parameter was 16.35% lower than in the healthy group. Notable differences were observed in the tolerance parameter for the duration of sustained cognitive effort: 57.9% of healthy volunteers sustained 100% of the effort duration, compared with 6.1% of volunteers with schizophrenia.

papers.title: A unified fixed-wavelet transformer decodes eight EEG classes across motor imagery, P300, and SSVEP paradigms.
papers.abstract: Motor imagery (MI) can support self-initiated control, whereas brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) based on the P300 or the steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) rely on ongoing visual stimulation. Repetitive visual stimulation can cause visual fatigue; when the stimuli are suspended, however, the corresponding P300 and SSVEP responses can no longer be elicited, and these paradigms alone cannot support a self-initiated command to restart visual stimulation. By contrast, self-initiated MI can provide a voluntary gating signal for switching visual stimulation on or off. Developing a single architecture capable of learning these heterogeneous EEG signatures and decoding multiple user intentions is therefore an important step toward a voluntarily controlled hybrid BCI. To this end, we developed a unified model by extending our previously proposed Analformer, a Transformer-based architecture designed for high classification performance while enabling the analysis of neurophysiologically meaningful EEG representations through AnalNet. We evaluated whether the model could classify EEG trials into eight mutually exclusive classes drawn from MI, P300, and SSVEP paradigms in the OpenBMI dataset. Analformer uses fixed Morlet wavelet kernels to extract frequency-specific EEG features, six Transformer blocks model dependencies across 31 pooled temporal tokens, and a two-stage training procedure to capture both population-level and participant-specific features. Across 54 participants, the mean accuracy obtained from the model after participant-specific fine-tuning was 71.00%, compared with 54.53% for EEG-Conformer, 52.30% for EEGNet, and 45.35% for ShallowConvNet under the same evaluation protocol. Ablation analyses showed that replacing the fixed wavelets with learnable convolutions reduced the mean accuracy to 63.15%, whereas omitting the two-stage training procedure reduced it to 47.38%. AnalNet, the built-in analysis module of Analformer, identified class-discriminative patterns, including sensorimotor mu- and beta-band activity during MI and stimulus-locked occipital responses during SSVEP. Together, these findings indicate that a single Transformer-based architecture can distinguish heterogeneous EEG classes and provide a foundation for unified decoding in hybrid BCIs that combine self-initiated MI gating with P300- and SSVEP-based command selection.

papers.title: Lesion-directed quantitative EEG after reperfusion therapy is associated with malignant cerebral edema and functional outcomes in acute ischemic stroke: a prospective exploratory cohort study.
papers.abstract: Ischemic stroke causes electrophysiological slowing within minutes which may precede detectable structural changes, making electroencephalography (EEG) a sensitive bedside marker of tissue at risk. Prior quantitative EEG (qEEG) studies often averaged bilateral or frontal activity, focused on thrombectomy, and were recorded at 24 h. We tested whether a lesion-directed alpha-to-delta ratio (lesion-ADR) within 72 h after reperfusion is associated with malignant cerebral edema (MCE) and functional outcomes. In a prospective single-center cohort of anterior-circulation ischemic stroke treated with intravenous alteplase (IV-rtPA), endovascular thrombectomy (EVT), or both, a 7-min EEG was obtained ≤72 h after reperfusion. Lesion-ADR was defined as the mean ADR of ipsilesional electrodes; the reperfusion-to-EEG interval (ΔT) was recorded. The primary outcome was MCE (midline shift ≥5 mm and/or decompressive hemicraniectomy). Secondary outcomes were favorable functional outcomes at discharge and 90 days (modified Rankin Scale [mRS] 0-2). Model discrimination was assessed using ROC analysis and AUC with bootstrap internal validation. Adjusted associations were assessed using parsimonious Firth penalized logistic regression models. Forty-nine patients were included. For MCE, the combined lesion-ADR + ΔT model achieved an apparent AUC of 0.888 (95% CI 0.765-0.960); bootstrap internal validation yielded an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.889. For discharge independence (mRS ≤ 2; n = 9), the ADR-only model showed an apparent AUC of 0.899. Lesion-ADR remained associated with favorable outcome after separate adjustment for admission NIHSS (OR 1.438 per 0.1-unit increase; p = 0.009) and reperfusion treatment modality (OR 1.367; p = 0.022). For 90-day independence (n = 13), the ADR-only AUC was 0.759 (95% CI 0.615-0.869) and the ADR-only model showed moderate discrimination for 90-day functional independence. The association with 90-day outcome was attenuated after accounting for admission NIHSS (OR 1.245 per 0.1-unit increase; p = 0.088). A brief lesion-directed ADR obtained within 72 h after reperfusion was associated with functional outcomes, while its combination with EEG timing showed encouraging discrimination for MCE in this cohort. These exploratory findings suggest lesion-directed qEEG may serve as a potential adjunctive biomarker after reperfusion therapy and warrant validation in larger cohorts.

papers.title: Systematic review of machine and deep learning in EEG Alzheimer's detection.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease is the most prevalent neurodegenerative disease, resulting in progressive memory loss in people. It has a significant impact on the population and the global healthcare system. Disease acquisition is a major concern due to the absence of pre-existing treatment options. The growth of machine learning and deep learning-based algorithms is effective in analyzing EEG data for diagnosing Alzheimer's disease. This systematic literature review investigates existing primary studies that focus on applying ML and DL in the identification of Alzheimer's disease, with emphasis on pre-processing, feature extraction, and classification. In doing so, it assesses the results produced by varying algorithms and addresses the problems encountered while deploying these systems. The review's objective is to offer a current situation and potential solutions for practitioners and scholars interested in healthcare service issues.

papers.title: Single-cell dataset of juvenile mouse neurons from the thalamic reticular nucleus: whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology.
papers.abstract: This dataset provides single-cell whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology for 19 interneurons of the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) in juvenile mice. The recordings were obtained from male C57Bl/6J mice sampled within the developmental window of postnatal days 24 to 34. Acute horizontal brain slices were used, and visually targeted whole-cell recordings were performed in current-clamp mode. A standardized current-clamp stimulus battery was used identically across all cells to characterize their intrinsic electrophysiological properties-passive membrane behavior, action-potential threshold and waveform, suprathreshold firing patterns, and the hyperpolarization-evoked rebound-burst dynamics characteristic of reticular thalamic neurons. The release comprises 18,015 recorded sweeps and their full, un-decimated signal traces (400 million digitized samples), preserved in the community-standard NWB (icephys) format alongside the original Igor Pro source files, and indexed into tidy, queryable Apache Parquet tables-one record per recording session, one per sweep, and one per digitized sample-linked by a normalized recording identifier. Each recording includes animal metadata (postnatal age, body weight, strain, genotype, slice orientation, and recorded region) and its resting membrane potential. The dataset is released as a FAIR² Data Package under the Open Data Commons Attribution License v1.0 (ODC-By v1.0), with machine-readable metadata conforming to the MLCommons Croissant specification, QUDT units, and PROV-O provenance. It is intended for neuroscientists, computational modelers, and machine-learning researchers studying the intrinsic electrophysiology of TRN neurons.

papers.title: The Effects of Methylphenidate on the EEG of Children with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder.
papers.abstract: AimsAttention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (AD/HD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder, with the symptom profile consisting of hyperactivity, impulsivity and inattention. Currently methylphenidate is the most widely used treatment for AD/HD. Studies on mixed stimulant use have found that stimulants result in normalisation of electroencephalogram (EEG) activity during an eyes-closed resting condition. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of Methylphenidate alone on the EEG of children with AD/HD and to extend the investigation into the gamma band.MethodFifty children with AD/HD and 50 typically developing children, between the ages of 8 and 12 years, participated in this study. Clinical participants were assessed for AD/HD at an initial session at which an EEG was performed. They returned within 1 week for a medication assessment, and a second EEG was recorded 1.5 h after ingestion of 10 mg of methylphenidate. EEG was recorded during an eyes-closed resting condition, and Fourier transformed to provide absolute and relative power estimates in delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma bands.ResultsUnmedicated, the AD/HD group had elevated global absolute and relative delta, elevated posterior absolute theta, elevated posterior relative theta, reduced global relative alpha, and reduced global absolute and relative gamma activity compared to the control group. Methylphenidate ingestion was associated with a global increase in absolute and relative beta, and in relative gamma activity.ConclusionsSignificant increases in fast wave activity were observed with methylphenidate use. However, unlike past research, it is not clear that this should be considered as normalisation of the EEG.
