papers.title: Under-recognized Autoimmune Encephalitis in Patients with Alzheimer's Disease: A Case Series Emphasizing EEG Screening.
papers.abstract: AD and AE present overlapping cognitive decline, often causing misdiagnosis and delayed immunotherapy. AD has an insidious onset and slow progression with typical Aβ and tau abnormalities, while AE manifests subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms and inflammatory imaging or CSF changes. Rapid cognitive decline in AD patients with superimposed AE is easily misdiagnosed as simple neurodegeneration. EEG is a convenient non-invasive test that can serve as a screening tool to trigger further autoimmune evaluation in AD patients with unexplained rapid deterioration. This case series reports two verified AD patients complicated with anti-LGI1 encephalitis and probable seronegative AE. It adds to the literature on the pathological coexistence and interaction of AD and AE, highlights the underutilized diagnostic value of EEG, and supports routine EEG screening for rapidly progressive AD cognitive decline. Two biomarker-confirmed AD female patients with comorbid AE were included. The 75-year-old patient had 4 years of cognitive decline (baseline MMSE=10), with typical AD imaging and biomarker abnormalities, positive anti-LGI1 IgG and abnormal EEG, diagnosed with AD combined with LGI1 encephalitis. She received IVIg, rituximab, anti-amyloid and anti-dementia treatment. MMSE improved from 10 to 18 at 1 month but fluctuated thereafter (MMSE 11-12, MoCA 3-9) with treatment pause and irregular adherence; serum LGI1 antibody and AD biomarkers remained normal throughout. The 62-year-old patient had 7 years of cognitive decline, personality changes, and hallucinations (MMSE=0, MoCA=0). She was diagnosed with probable seronegative AE complicated with AD based on AD imaging changes, positive CSF indicators, and positive TBA findings. Treatment with telitacicept and lecanemab was associated with modest cognitive improvement (MMSE +3, MoCA +2) at short-term follow-up. Rapid cognitive exacerbation in AD patients should not be attributed to natural neurodegeneration. Routine EEG is an essential noninvasive tool for cognitive evaluation in AD. EEG abnormalities in AD patients require comprehensive autoimmune examinations. Concurrent AE is a reversible and treatable factor worsening AD cognitive impairment. Combined immunotherapy and anti-amyloid treatment can significantly improve patient cognition and biomarkers. EEG should be a routine screening item for rapidly progressive AD. Autoimmune inflammation may accelerate AD progression, providing new insights for AD immunological pathogenesis and targeted therapy research.

papers.title: The association between depressive symptoms, physical activity, flow state, and resting-state EEG in college students.
papers.abstract: Exploring the correlations among physical activity, flow state, and resting-state EEG in college students with depressive symptoms. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 216 college students. Participants completed questionnaires assessing depressive symptoms, physical exercise, and flow proneness, followed by a 5-min resting-state EEG recording. Group differences and associations were examined using independent-samples t-tests, χ² tests, Pearson correlations, and regression-based serial mediation analyses. The primary mediation models were adjusted for sex and self-rated physical health, with unadjusted models reported for comparison. Physical exercise was associated with fewer depressive symptoms and greater flow proneness, and significant frontal EEG lateralization differences were observed between students with and without depressive symptoms. In the unadjusted mediation analyses, significant indirect effects were observed through Fp2/Fp1 δ- and α2-band lateralization and through the serial EEG lateralization-flow pathways. However, after adjustment for sex and self-rated physical health, the EEG-related indirect effects were no longer statistically significant in either the δ- or α2-band model. In contrast, the indirect effect through flow proneness alone remained significant in both adjusted models (Ind2), indicating that the flow-related indirect association was more robust to covariate adjustment than the EEG-related pathways. There is a close correlation among physical activities, EEG-specific indicators and the state of flow. However, whether the EEG-specific indicators play a mediating role remains to be further verified.

papers.title: Interrupted-Sampling Repeater Jamming Suppression for Frequency-Agile Radar Based on Time-Frequency Analysis and Multi-Domain Filtering.
papers.abstract: Interrupted-sampling repeater jamming (ISRJ) produces coherent false targets after pulse compression and degrades the reliability of frequency-agile radar sensors, particularly at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and high jamming-to-signal ratio (JSR). Existing single-domain suppression methods often provide insufficient separation between jamming and target echoes and may attenuate target-bearing components. This paper proposes a joint time-frequency analysis and multi-domain filtering method for radar waveforms employing intra-pulse and inter-pulse frequency agility. A forwarded jamming segment retains the carrier frequency of the sampled sub-pulse while overlapping a subsequent sub-pulse with a different carrier frequency, producing a joint displacement in time and frequency relative to the genuine target echo. Based on this property, a sub-pulse-wise two-dimensional feature extraction strategy is developed in the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) domain. Empirical probability density criteria are derived from projections along the time and frequency axes to determine adaptive rejection thresholds. The resulting time-selective and frequency-selective rejection regions are combined through logical intersection to construct a two-dimensional notch filter. The retained components are reconstructed using the inverse STFT and processed by segmented pulse compression. Simulations covering direct, periodic, and cyclic ISRJ show that the proposed method suppresses coherent false targets while limiting the loss of pulse-compression gain. It achieves higher peak signal-to-jamming-plus-noise ratios than the reference method over the tested SNR and JSR ranges and remains effective under adverse conditions. The proposed method improves the interference resilience of frequency-agile radar sensors and provides more reliable target echoes for subsequent detection and parameter estimation.
